Its contents cover business operations, R&D, products and markets, intellectual property, competition, pricing, regulation, environmental matters, personnel, risks, cybersecurity, properties and legal matters; market and financial results, risk disclosures, financial statements and controls; governance, directors, executive compensation, ownership and related-party matters; and exhibits, schedules, and signatures.

title: DEFINED TERMS
summary: Defines terminology used in Pfizer’s 2023 Form 10-K, including fiscal-year conventions and a broad glossary of financial, medical, regulatory, business, product, partner, and organizational abbreviations and names. It clarifies emergency-use status and limitations for specified COVID-19 vaccines and Paxlovid, cautions that clinical-study discussions require broader context and regulatory interpretation, and notes rounding and trademark conventions. It explains where SEC filings, proxy materials, ESG reports, investor and governance information, and shareholder services are available, which online content is not incorporated by reference, and how investors can follow disclosures or request governance materials.

It then introduces Pfizer as a global research-based biopharmaceutical company, describing its products and services, patient-access mission, corporate purpose and principles, six ESG priorities, and growth strategy centered on its pipeline, existing products, and business development.

title: Business Risks: Regulation, Litigation, IP and Security
summary: The page outlines business risks from competitive pricing pressures; foreign laws and government price or access controls; legal, environmental and tax litigation, costs, outcomes and reserves; and changing regulations, tax rules and global minimum taxation. It also covers IT outages, cyberattacks, theft, extortion, AI-related challenges, patent application and extension delays, and intellectual-property disputes or government and stakeholder actions that could limit protection or enforcement, including for Comirnaty and Paxlovid.

title: ABOUT PFIZER
summary: Pfizer is a Delaware-incorporated global biopharmaceutical company focused on discovering, developing, manufacturing and commercializing therapies worldwide, while collaborating to improve access to healthcare. Most revenue comes from medicines and vaccines; the company also sells diagnostic products and provides R&D services. It seeks to improve health outcomes, expand patient access and manage pricing and contracting. Its purpose is “Breakthroughs that change patients’ lives,” guided by five principles: trust, science, innovation, urgency and execution. Its ESG strategy covers innovation, equitable access and pricing, product quality and safety, diversity and inclusion, climate change, and ethics. Growth priorities include advancing its pipeline, maximizing existing products and pursuing business development. Pfizer completed its Seagen acquisition in December 2023, adding four cancer medicines and a broad range of oncology modalities, and divested its early-stage rare-disease gene therapy portfolio to Alexion in September 2023.

title: COMMERCIAL OPERATIONS
summary: In 2023, Pfizer operated globally through Biopharma and Business Innovation (PC1 and Pfizer Ignite), with Biopharma the sole reportable segment and organized around Primary Care, Specialty Care and Oncology. At the start of 2024, it reorganized Biopharma to integrate Seagen into Oncology, U.S. Commercial and International Commercial divisions. The text describes each division’s scope and therapeutic portfolios, lists representative oncology, primary care and specialty care products, and directs readers to segment/product revenue disclosures, revenue-driver analysis and risks from reliance on major products.

title: RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
key_items: Our R&D Priorities and Strategy; Our R&D Operations; Our R&D Pipeline
summary: Pfizer’s R&D aims to develop impactful medicines and vaccines and improve existing products’ safety, efficacy, dosing, and indications. Priorities include differentiated therapies, long-term capabilities, and flexible partnerships; work centers on six therapeutic areas and combines internal research with external collaborations, licenses, investments, and acquisitions. In 2023, Pfizer reorganized R&D into oncology-focused ORD and other-area PRD, with company-wide portfolio oversight and resource allocation; expenses are not reported by phase or area. Drug development can exceed ten years and is costly and unpredictable; pipeline and candidate details and related risks are covered elsewhere in the filing.

title: COLLABORATION AND CO-PROMOTION AGREEMENTS
summary: Pfizer describes collaboration and co-promotion agreements that support development, R&D, sales and distribution. It outlines arrangements for Comirnaty with BioNTech; Eliquis with BMS; Xtandi and Padcev with Astellas; and Orgovyx and Myfembree with SMPA, including cost, profit, royalty, market, commercialization, regulatory and supply responsibilities. It also notes arrangements for Adcetris and Tivdak following the Seagen acquisition and collaborations on pipeline products. Related revenues are generally classified as Alliance revenues, with exceptions for direct sales and most Comirnaty and Padcev revenues; further details are referenced elsewhere in the filing.

title: INTERNATIONAL OPERATIONS
summary: The company operates globally, supplying medicines and vaccines to about 200 countries and territories. Emerging markets are central to its growth strategy, supported by urbanization, a growing middle class, and economic shifts. Outside the U.S., 2023 revenue was $31.4 billion (54% of total); revenue exceeded $500 million in 14 countries in 2023, versus 24 in 2022 and 21 in 2021, with the decline mainly due to lower Comirnaty and Paxlovid sales. Japan was the largest non-U.S. market in 2023. Geographic revenue details and risks of international operations are covered elsewhere in the report.

title: SALES AND MARKETING
summary: Pfizer sells prescription biopharmaceuticals mainly to wholesalers, with Paxlovid largely sold to governments in 2022–2023; U.S. vaccines go to government, wholesalers, providers and pharmacies, while international vaccines go to institutions. Government contracts for Comirnaty and Paxlovid generated significant revenue, though some government contracts may change or end; U.S. sales shifted to commercial channels in late 2023. Pfizer seeks formulary access and collaborates with payors on disease education. It promotes approved product uses, benefits and risks to providers, patients, insurers, employers and governments through direct-to-consumer and public-health advertising, patient assistance, and virtual and in-person engagement.

title: PATENTS AND OTHER INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY RIGHTS
summary: Pfizer describes its patent and licensing rights, how patent terms and protection vary by country, possible extensions and regulatory exclusivity, and a table of key products with U.S., European and Japanese patent-expiry estimates and qualifications. Notes explain pending extensions, litigation, collaborations, regional commercialization and royalties, and product-specific patent or exclusivity details. The text warns that loss or expiry of rights can trigger lower-priced generic or biosimilar competition and reduce revenue, with moderate effects expected in 2024–2025 and greater effects in 2026–2030; Pfizer defends its rights while considering patient access. It also describes renewable trademark and trade-dress protection.

title: COMPETITION
summary: The text describes intense competition in regulated markets based on product efficacy, safety, convenience and cost, from global and smaller biopharma companies, generics and biosimilars. Competitor R&D, patent challenges and product launches threaten sales and product relevance. Pfizer responds with major R&D and business-development investment, post-approval research, stakeholder education, effective commercialization, organizational adaptation, ethical practices, affordability and access initiatives—including its 2022 Accord for a Healthier World. It highlights vaccine and biosimilar competition and Pfizer’s aim to launch biosimilars early. Generics benefit from lower costs, streamlined approvals, payer preference and substitution rules; China’s QCE and VBP programs intensify pressure. Biosimilars offer lower-cost, highly similar biologics and are regulated by the FDA in the U.S. and EMA in the EU.

title: PRICING PRESSURES AND MANAGED CARE ORGANIZATIONS
summary: The text describes commercial pricing pressures from high-deductible plans, payor bargaining, rebates, competition, insurer/PBM consolidation, and purchaser discount demands, which can reduce prices, coverage, access, and demand. It discusses the shift toward outcomes-based and risk-sharing payments, their potential benefits and drawbacks, uncertain adoption after COVID-19, and equity and financial-resilience goals. Pfizer outlines advocacy, affordability, payor engagement, and efforts to demonstrate product value. It also explains MCO growth and consolidation, formulary and utilization controls, patient cost-sharing, cost-management priorities, competition for coverage, and risks to product demand and financial performance.

title: RAW MATERIALS
summary: The company sources essential raw materials from numerous global suppliers, generally with sufficient quantities and multiple sources. No significant availability-related operational impact is anticipated in 2024, though heightened industry demand for some components and materials could constrain supply and affect the business. The company monitors risks and mitigates them through supplier management, qualifying additional suppliers, and advance purchasing where possible.

In the U.S., FDA and other agencies regulate product development, approval, manufacturing, promotion, safety monitoring, and supply chains; emergency authorizations and biosimilar exclusivity rules are also outlined. It covers healthcare fraud-and-abuse and marketing laws, government pricing and reimbursement programs, and IRA measures—including Medicare discounts, inflation rebates, negotiated prices, and Eliquis selection—whose effects and legal status remain uncertain. Potential Medicaid and 340B changes could also materially affect the business.

It describes biosimilar approval and reference-product exclusivity periods, and federal and state rules against healthcare fraud and abuse, false claims, improper financial interactions, and deceptive drug marketing.

nodes.title: Pricing, Reimbursement and Access Regulations
nodes.summary: The text describes U.S. and international regulation affecting Pfizer’s pricing, reimbursement, market access, product approvals, safety monitoring, anti-corruption compliance, and data privacy. U.S. coverage includes government discounts and price reporting; the IRA’s Medicare benefit changes, rebates, and drug-price negotiations; Medicaid and 340B rulemaking, litigation, and Pfizer’s contract-pharmacy integrity policy; state formulary and rebate controls; and broader government and commercial payer efforts to curb costs. It notes possible business and compliance impacts. Outside the U.S., it outlines EU, U.K., Japanese, Chinese, and other-market approval systems, proposed EU pharmaceutical reforms, EU pharmacovigilance and growing international safety regulation, and government influence over medicine pricing and reimbursement.

nodes.title: Regulatory, Pricing, Privacy, and Drug Approval Issues
nodes.summary: The text outlines 340B contract-pharmacy policy disputes, state and federal enforcement risks, and Medicaid and broader drug-pricing pressures from governments, payors, and industry consolidation. It describes anti-corruption laws and evolving privacy and data-security obligations, including breach-related penalties and reputational risks. Outside the U.S., it explains drug approval pathways and regulators in the EU, U.K., Japan, China, and other markets; proposed EU pharmaceutical reforms; and pharmacovigilance oversight and its expansion.

nodes.title: Pricing and Reimbursement
nodes.summary: The text discusses global pharmaceutical pricing and reimbursement controls, including China’s cost-containment, negotiation and tendering measures and Pfizer’s unsuccessful bids for certain products; healthcare-provider payment disclosure rules; worldwide intellectual-property protections, threats and advocacy; evolving privacy laws and risks; and environmental compliance, cleanup spending, expected financial effects, and Pfizer’s 2040 net-zero and emissions-reduction goals.

nodes.title: Global Pricing, Transparency, IP and Data Privacy
nodes.summary: The text describes global and China-specific drug-pricing controls, reimbursement negotiations, procurement and quality evaluation, resulting access and business uncertainties, and WHO initiatives. It covers disclosure requirements for company transfers of value to healthcare providers and organizations; worldwide patent protections, challenges, policy changes and advocacy; and evolving, inconsistent privacy laws governing sensitive data, with growing enforcement and risks of fines, litigation and reputational harm from noncompliance or breaches.

summary: The section covers extensive U.S. and international regulation of Pfizer’s products, operations, research, manufacturing, marketing, safety monitoring, supply chains, healthcare interactions, and data, including FDA approvals and emergency authorizations, biosimilar exclusivity, fraud-and-abuse and transparency rules, and anti-corruption requirements. It details government and private-payer pricing, reimbursement, discounts, rebates, IRA negotiations, Medicaid, 340B, state controls, and global procurement and cost-containment measures, including China’s. It also addresses evolving drug-approval and pharmacovigilance systems, intellectual-property protections and challenges, privacy and cybersecurity obligations, and environmental compliance and emissions goals, noting uncertainties, costs, enforcement, and potential business and reputational impacts.

title: ENVIRONMENTAL MATTERS
summary: Pfizer is subject to environmental laws, funds compliance, and cleans up contamination from past industrial activity. In 2023, it spent $92 million on environmental capital expenditures and $158 million on other environmental expenses; such costs are not currently expected to materially affect its financial position. Pfizer targets a 95% reduction in its own GHG emissions and a 90% reduction in value-chain emissions from 2019 levels by 2040, aligning with the Science Based Targets initiative’s Net-Zero Standard. Its developing reduction plan includes new technologies, climate solutions, and supplier targets. 2023 plan spending was not material; near-term financial effects are not expected to be material, though longer-term impacts are uncertain. The text refers readers to the climate-change and sustainability risk discussion.

summary: Pfizer describes its 2023 workforce, purpose, and efforts to attract, retain, engage, and support colleagues, including workforce demographics and competitive, wellness-focused employment. It outlines its core values—Courage, Excellence, Equity, and Joy—and DEI initiatives spanning workplace inclusion, health equity, partnerships, and representative clinical trials. Engagement efforts include feedback channels, the Pfizer Pulse survey, improved teamwork and decision-making, and Bravo recognition. The text also covers leadership expectations and performance reviews, non-linear career growth and learning opportunities, global EHS protections and wellness services, and annual public reporting on equitable pay.

title: ITEM 1A. RISK FACTORS
summary: The section cautions that the listed material business risks, considered alongside the report and other SEC filings, are not exhaustive or fully predictable. The company also faces general risks, including economic conditions, geopolitical events, extreme weather, and natural disasters. If known or unknown risks materialize, they could materially harm current or future operations, financial condition, results, cash flows, prospects, reputation, or credit ratings. The discussion includes forward-looking statements.

title: RISKS RELATED TO OUR BUSINESS, INDUSTRY AND OPERATIONS:

nodes.title: MANAGED CARE TRENDS
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks from managed-care cost controls, consolidation, formularies, rebates, utilization restrictions, IRA-related pricing pressure, and regulatory scrutiny of payor arrangements. It describes competition from innovative, generic, and biosimilar products, patent challenges and expiries, and factors limiting biosimilar uptake. Revenue concentration in nine products (including Comirnaty), COVID-19 revenue declines, product-specific risks, and dependence on significant customers create exposure. Finally, it emphasizes ongoing R&D and replenishment of products through internal development and external partnerships to offset losses and support growth.

nodes.title: Competitive Products and Revenue Concentration
nodes.summary: Discusses risks from government scrutiny of business arrangements and competition, including branded and generic drugs, biosimilars, patent challenges and expirations, pricing pressure, and barriers to biosimilar uptake. Highlights revenue concentration in nine products, especially Comirnaty, and risks from declining demand, safety or regulatory issues, litigation, competition, supply and access pressures, and COVID-19 revenue declines. Also notes customer concentration and increased pricing pressure from pharmacy-chain and wholesaler consolidation.

nodes.title: RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
nodes.summary: Pfizer must continually develop new products and uses to replace lost exclusivity or market share, meet healthcare trends, and support growth, relying on internal R&D and external partnerships or transactions. Success depends on identifying promising, reimbursable treatments, while balancing investment, current growth, and shareholder returns amid rising development costs and regulatory demands. Early decisions affect trial design, marketing, and reimbursement, and optimal trial outcomes cannot be assured. Candidates may fail, receive no approval, or prove uncompetitive; poor scientific choices or resource allocation can weaken the pipeline. Novel gene therapies pose particular uncertainty in development time, cost, and approval.

nodes.title: GLOBAL OPERATIONS
nodes.summary: The company’s global operations face risks from currency and interest-rate movements, economic and political instability, government actions and regulation, conflicts, public-health emergencies, natural disasters and climate impacts. Emerging-market instability and limited healthcare resources may undermine growth and counterparties’ ability to pay or perform. Government cost controls can pressure prices; trade restrictions or tariffs may reduce sales, raise costs and create financial, pension, counterparty and credit-loss risks. International operations generated 54% of 2023 revenue (24% Europe; 20% Japan, China and Asia Pacific), exposing results, assets and financial guidance to exchange rates and inflation. Borrowings, benefit obligations and investments also face interest- and exchange-rate risks; related disclosures are referenced in MD&A and notes.

nodes.title: PRODUCT MANUFACTURING, SALES AND MARKETING RISKS
nodes.summary: Pfizer describes risks from manufacturing, supply-chain, distribution, sales and marketing disruptions, regulatory inspections and noncompliance, including the 2021 Chantix recall and expected 2024 submissions concerning its return outside the U.S., and tornado damage to its Rocky Mount facility affecting supply through 2024. It outlines dependence on collaborators and service providers, whose failures or disruptions may harm development, operations, revenues and reputation. Counterfeit medicines threaten patients, trust and sales despite mitigation efforts. Pricing and reimbursement risks include expanding global price controls, U.S. IRA Medicare negotiations and rebates, legal uncertainty, payer and state cost-containment measures, and pressure from generics, biosimilars and industry consolidation.

nodes.title: Supply, Third-Party Dependencies, and Counterfeit Risks
key_items: COLLABORATIONS AND OTHER RELATIONSHIPS WITH THIRD PARTIES
nodes.summary: A tornado damaged Pfizer’s Rocky Mount facility in July 2023; manufacturing resumed, but affected medicine supplies may remain disrupted through 2024. Pfizer relies on third parties and business-development arrangements across research, manufacturing, and commercialization, exposing it to delays, compliance, quality, supply, cyber, operational, and reputational risks; collaboration expirations may reduce alliance revenue. Counterfeit medicines threaten patient safety, trust, and sales, with e-commerce and pandemic-era online access increasing exposure. Pfizer uses education, technology, monitoring, law enforcement, and policy engagement to combat counterfeits, but these efforts may not prevent their continued growth.

summary: The section covers risks from managed-care controls, pricing and reimbursement pressures, regulation, consolidation, competition, patent challenges and expirations, and revenue concentration in key products and customers, including declining COVID-19 sales. It discusses dependence on successful R&D, internal and partnered development, clinical and regulatory uncertainty, and the need to replenish the portfolio. It also addresses global economic, political, currency, interest-rate, trade, climate and public-health risks; manufacturing and supply disruptions, inspections and compliance; third-party dependencies and collaboration risks; and counterfeit medicines.

title: RISKS RELATED TO GOVERNMENT REGULATION AND LEGAL PROCEEDINGS:

nodes.title: PRICING AND REIMBURSEMENT
nodes.summary: Government price controls, coverage restrictions, and reimbursement policies in the U.S. and internationally may reduce access, pricing, and revenue; global drug and vaccine cost-containment pressures are expected to persist. The U.S. IRA introduces Medicare price negotiations and maximum fair prices, inflation-linked rebates, and a revised Part D discount program; Eliquis is selected for a 2026 price, while legal challenges leave some effects uncertain. Generic and biosimilar promotion, payer consolidation, state measures, and drug-importation policies add pressure. Other markets use price controls, tenders, and access rules, including China’s price-cutting tenders and proposed EU reforms; vaccine tender outcomes matter. COVID-related budget deficits further intensify pressures.

nodes.title: U.S. HEALTHCARE REGULATION
nodes.summary: The U.S. healthcare industry is highly regulated and subject to frequent change; federal or state reforms to care delivery or funding could materially affect the company. Other potential adverse actions include budget controls, patent-law changes, drug importation, revised government biopharmaceutical reimbursement or discounts, limits on stakeholder interactions, and cost-focused comparative-effectiveness policies restricting innovative medicines. Spending cuts to Medicare, Medicaid, or other public programs, including implementation of the IRA, could reduce payment for products and services. Further federal and state cost-containment measures are expected; commercial payors may follow Medicare policies, and coverage and reimbursement can become less favorable even after initially favorable decisions.

nodes.title: DEVELOPMENT, REGULATORY APPROVAL AND MARKETING OF PRODUCTS
nodes.summary: Drug, vaccine and biologic development is costly, lengthy, unpredictable and risky, with potential delays or failure from trial recruitment challenges, unfavorable or reinterpreted data, protocol changes, missed milestones, and inability to address regulators’ comments or obtain approval. Approval depends on safety and efficacy assessments and may be conditional or accelerated, requiring confirmatory studies. Regulatory or advisory decisions, changing requirements, safety or efficacy concerns, impurities, labeling or population restrictions, manufacturing issues, recalls, withdrawals, litigation, and expanded trial or post-approval obligations can delay approval, raise costs, or harm product availability and commercial prospects.

nodes.title: POST-AUTHORIZATION/APPROVAL DATA
nodes.summary: FDA and foreign regulators may require or sponsors may undertake post-approval studies; findings or emerging safety data can affect approval, labeling, safety or efficacy concerns, and commercial availability, including risks shared across a product class. Impacts may take time to assess, and requirements vary by jurisdiction. Comirnaty’s EUA requires observational studies assessing specified adverse events, deaths, hospitalizations, and severe COVID-19 across designated and other populations; FDA approval also carries postmarketing commitments through 2024 and beyond. Paxlovid’s EUA genomic-variant monitoring and reporting requirements were removed after becoming NDA postmarketing commitments; FDA also required assessment of activity against variants of interest and other analyses and studies.

nodes.title: LEGAL MATTERS
nodes.summary: Pfizer faces unpredictable litigation and investigations involving patents, products, securities, competition, contracts, environmental, tax, employment, and other matters, which may cause significant financial, operational, or reputational harm. Patent losses could remove product protection and reduce sales. Government enforcement may bring fines, criminal charges, business restrictions, agreements, and penalties, including in qui tam suits. Extensive U.S. and international rules govern sales, marketing, pricing, healthcare-provider interactions, and product information; inquiries and claims, including risks amplified by digital marketing, can lead to costs and reputational damage. Pfizer’s 2018 OIG Corporate Integrity Agreement expired in May 2023, and its final report awaits response. Legal and environmental liabilities rely on uncertain estimates, and costs may exceed accruals; further details appear in Note 16A.

summary: The section describes risks from government regulation and legal proceedings, including U.S. and international price controls, reimbursement restrictions, tenders, generic competition, and reforms such as the IRA that may reduce access, prices, and revenue. Changing healthcare laws and spending cuts could further constrain payments and coverage. Costly, uncertain product development and approval can be delayed or curtailed by trial, regulatory, safety, efficacy, manufacturing, or labeling issues; post-approval studies and emerging data may also affect product status and availability. Litigation and investigations across patents, products, marketing, pricing, and other matters may cause financial, operational, or reputational harm, penalties, restrictions, or liabilities exceeding estimates.

title: RISKS RELATED TO INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY, TECHNOLOGY AND SECURITY:
summary: The text outlines risks from inadequate intellectual-property protection, including unsuccessful or delayed patents, changing laws, country-specific enforcement, compulsory licensing, generic and biosimilar challenges, litigation, loss of licenses, and trademark or trade-secret misuse. It also covers third-party patent disputes and infringement claims that can delay launches, impose damages or royalties, or halt sales, including risks from at-risk launches and expanding mRNA products. IT and cybersecurity risks include outages, data breaches, sophisticated attacks, third-party and supply-chain vulnerabilities, and potentially insufficient insurance, causing operational, financial, legal, and reputational harm. AI tools also pose risks from flawed or biased data and accidental disclosure of confidential information.

title: GENERAL RISKS

nodes.title: BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT ACTIVITIES AND STRATEGIC GOALS
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks from Pfizer’s growth strategy and business-development transactions, including competition, execution and integration failures, missed revenue, savings or accretion targets, liabilities, financing needs, and substantial Seagen-related debt that may constrain flexibility and cash flow. Third-party securities investments may lose value and be difficult to sell. It also describes pandemic-related operational, demand, supply-chain, workforce, economic and forecasting risks. COVID-19 uncertainty affects planning and financial projections, while vaccine and treatment efforts face demand and inventory risks, commercialization and supply challenges, clinical and safety uncertainties, variant effectiveness, data interpretation, and regulatory submission, approval and authorization uncertainties.

nodes.title: PANDEMICS
nodes.summary: Investments in third-party debt or equity securities, including Haleon, may provide no influence over the companies, fluctuate or lose value, and may be difficult to sell or distribute at an acceptable price—or at all—depending on market conditions and ownership stake. Pandemics such as COVID-19 may harm business, operations, financial condition and results through uncertainty about severity and duration; operational impacts and lower demand; higher costs; manufacturing, supply-chain and third-party-supplier disruptions or shortages; macroeconomic, labor-market and talent challenges; resources diverted to pandemic responses; difficulties forecasting performance; uncertain recovery and volatile financial or credit markets; and broader effects on financial performance.

nodes.title: COVID-19
nodes.summary: Pfizer cannot predict COVID-19’s future effects on its business or finances, despite planning assumptions, and unknown risks may emerge. Its COVID-19 products face risks spanning endemic/seasonal demand, revenue forecasting, inventory write-offs and commercial transition; R&D, clinical data, safety, efficacy, variants and development timelines; regulatory submissions, approvals, labeling and recommendations; manufacturing, raw materials, supply, distribution and storage; competition, pricing, access, public confidence and medication errors; partnerships, funding and recovery of costs; trade restrictions, royalties and litigation. Some risks also apply to COVID-19 and influenza diagnostic tests.

nodes.title: CLIMATE CHANGE AND SUSTAINABILITY
nodes.summary: Pfizer faces climate-transition risks, including higher energy and compliance costs, and physical risks such as droughts, floods, wildfires, and extreme weather that may disrupt production and supply chains. A 2023 tornado damaged its Rocky Mount facility, with medicine supply effects expected through 2024. Pfizer targets voluntary net-zero emissions by 2040, but technology, investment, and policy constraints may hinder progress. Growing ESG expectations and reporting requirements may raise costs and affect competitiveness; failing, or appearing to fail, to meet goals or stakeholder expectations could damage reputation, demand, and operations.

title: ITEM 1C. CYBERSECURITY
summary: Pfizer integrates cybersecurity into its board-overseen enterprise risk management, using threat monitoring, safeguards, training, supplier controls, collaboration, incident-response plans, cross-functional coordination, and ongoing testing and independent assessments. The Audit Committee oversees the program and receives regular briefings; the CISO leads management’s response with business leaders. Pfizer reports no known incidents materially affecting or likely to materially affect it. The text also describes its 284 global properties (about 38 million square feet), including 37 manufacturing plants and Seagen-acquired sites, and notes they are suitable for foreseeable needs. Legal proceedings are discussed in Note 16A.

title: Cybersecurity, Properties, and Legal Proceedings

It summarizes global owned and leased properties, including headquarters, 284 sites totaling about 38 million square feet, Seagen additions, and 37 PGS manufacturing plants, noting their suitability. Legal proceedings are discussed in Note 16A.

It identifies acquisitions, fair value, revenues, asset impairments, tax assets and liabilities and income tax contingencies, pension and postretirement benefit plans, and legal and environmental contingencies as critical policies requiring especially subjective or complex judgments. Recently adopted accounting standards are discussed in Note 1B.

nodes.title: Acquisition Valuation and Revenue Deductions
nodes.summary: Explains acquisition accounting and fair-value methods for acquired intangible assets, inventory, and PP&E, including key assumptions and their potential effects on results. Seagen acquisition values remain provisional and will be finalized within one year. Describes estimates for product revenue deductions, their historical immateriality overall but possible impact on individual product trends, and greater adjustment risk for U.S. government and performance-based rebates due to settlement delays and product and channel mix.

nodes.title: Asset Impairments
nodes.summary: The text describes Pfizer’s impairment policies: ongoing review of long-lived assets, annual testing of goodwill and indefinite-lived intangibles, impairment indicators, and discounted-cash-flow valuation assumptions and vulnerable intangible assets. Goodwill testing begins with qualitative assessment, followed when needed by quantitative valuation; none was impaired in 2023. It also covers benefit-plan assumptions and their effects on costs, reports U.S. and international pension return and discount-rate data for 2021–2023, explains how expected returns and discount rates are determined, and provides sensitivity to a 50-basis-point return decline ($84 million higher 2024 costs) and 2023 asset gains ($835 million).

nodes.title: Goodwill Impairment and Benefit Plan Assumptions
key_items: Expected Annual Rate of Return on Plan Assets
nodes.summary: The page reports no goodwill impairment in 2023 and describes the qualitative screening and discounted-cash-flow approach used for impairment testing, key valuation assumptions, and factors that may affect future tests. It discusses benefit-plan assumptions and their impact on results, presents U.S. and international pension plans’ expected and actual asset returns and obligation discount rates for 2021–2023, and explains how expected returns are determined, applied, and remeasurement differences recognized. It also introduces a sensitivity analysis of 2024 benefit costs to a 50-basis-point reduction in expected returns.

nodes.title: Assumption
key_items: Discount Rate Used to Measure Plan Obligations
nodes.summary: A 50-basis-point decline in the expected annual return on plan assets has an estimated $84 impact, excluding potential mark-to-market adjustments; actual plan assets gained approximately $835 million in 2023. U.S. and significant international plan discount rates are reviewed at least annually using high-quality, investment-grade bonds and applicable local requirements. Year-end rates affect current-year actuarial gains or losses and the following year’s service and interest costs. The text introduces a sensitivity analysis of the effects of a 10-basis-point discount-rate decline on 2023 periodic benefit costs and 2024 benefit obligations, holding other assumptions constant.

nodes.title: Assumption

Income tax assets and liabilities include valuation allowances and accruals for uncertain tax positions, with further discussion in specified notes and MD&A. The company and certain subsidiaries face ordinary-course contingencies, including tax and legal matters, guarantees, and indemnifications, detailed in referenced notes.

Covers acquisition fair-value estimates, provisional Seagen valuations, and revenue deductions; impairment reviews and testing for long-lived assets, goodwill, and intangibles; and pension and postretirement assumptions, including asset returns, discount rates, reported experience, and sensitivity effects on costs and obligations. Also addresses income tax assets, liabilities, valuation allowances and uncertain tax positions, and legal, environmental, tax, guarantee, and indemnification contingencies.

Emerging-markets revenue declined 40%, chiefly from Comirnaty and Paxlovid. The text also explains estimated product-revenue deductions, presents 2021–2023 deduction categories and totals, attributes the 2023 increase in returns and discounts largely to a Paxlovid inventory revenue reversal, and notes deductions depend on sales, product mix and contractual or legislative terms.

Notes Comirnaty revenue scope, patent and litigation references, and product-indication notes. title: PRODUCT DEVELOPMENTS
summary: Pfizer reports its development pipeline as of January 30, 2024, explains the scope and timing of regulatory milestones, and summarizes updated XBB.1.5 COVID-19 vaccine approvals and authorizations by age group in the U.S., EU and Japan. summary: Pfizer explains its non-GAAP Adjusted income and Adjusted diluted EPS measures, their definitions, uses in evaluating recurring performance, forecasting, budgeting, and compensation, and their limitations versus GAAP and peers. It describes exclusions for intangible amortization, acquisition-related costs, discontinued operations, and significant items, including restructuring, impairments, securities and pension gains or losses, and unusual costs. title: ANALYSIS OF THE CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF CASH FLOWS
summary: The text refers readers to Pfizer’s 2022 Form 10-K for explanations of 2022 versus 2021 cash-flow changes and 2021 discontinued operations. For continuing operations, 2023 operating cash provided was $8.7 billion, down from $29.3 billion in 2022, mainly due to lower adjusted net income and payment timing, partly offset by inventory changes. Investing cash used was $32.3 billion, largely reflecting the $43.4 billion Seagen acquisition, versus 2022 acquisitions and a $4.0 billion joint-venture dividend; higher short-term investment redemptions and lower long-term investment purchases partly offset the change. summary: Pfizer describes its liquidity sources and cash-management practices, including operating cash flow, investments, credit facilities and market access, and financing for the Seagen acquisition. nodes.title: Basis, Standards, Estimates, and Acquisitions
key_items: B. New Accounting Standards Adopted in 2023
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s consolidated statements follow U.S. GAAP, describe consolidation and subsidiary reporting periods, segments, major transactions, reclassifications, and rounding. In 2023, Pfizer adopted supplier-finance disclosure and reference-rate-reform standards, including hedge-accounting expedients. The notes explain how estimates affect financial statement amounts, their uncertainty and regular review. Acquisitions are accounted for using fair values, with transaction costs expensed, goodwill recorded when applicable, acquired IPR&D treated according to whether a business was acquired, and contingent consideration remeasured through earnings.

nodes.title: E. Fair Value
nodes.summary: The text explains Pfizer’s fair-value measurement approach, using an orderly-market exit price from market participants’ perspectives, considering highest and best use for nonfinancial assets and unchanged nonperformance risk for liabilities. Valuation techniques include income, market, and cost approaches; inputs are classified as Levels 1, 2, or 3 according to observability. Financial instruments are valued using matrix pricing, quoted prices, observable NAVs, market data, yield curves, and currency prices; derivative credit risk was insignificant. Pfizer periodically reviews third-party pricing methods, inputs, and outputs for reasonableness through cross-checks, monitoring, and comparisons with actual sales.

nodes.title: F. Foreign Currency Translation
nodes.summary: Most international operations use local currencies as their functional currencies. Assets and liabilities are translated into U.S. dollars at balance-sheet-date rates, and income and expenses at period-average rates; resulting translation effects are recorded in other comprehensive income or loss. Conversion effects on nonfunctional-currency monetary items are recorded in other income or deductions, net. In highly inflationary economies, monetary items use balance-sheet-date rates, with adjustments recorded in other income or deductions, net, while nonmonetary items use historical rates.

nodes.title: G. Revenues and Trade Accounts Receivable
key_items: Revenue Recognition; Our Sales Contracts; Deductions from Revenues

It describes trade-receivable credit-loss estimation and write-offs; accounting for collaboration revenues, costs, milestones, and royalties; inventory valuation and impairment; selling and advertising, R&D, and acquired IPR&D expense; and depreciation and amortization of property and intangible assets.

The company reviews long-lived assets for impairment, testing goodwill and indefinite-lived intangibles annually and other assets when indicators arise, using asset-specific fair-value methods and reassessing useful lives or indefinite-lived status where applicable. Restructuring and acquisition-related costs include integration, transaction, facility, workforce, and productivity actions; employee costs are recorded when probable and estimable, transaction costs when incurred, and useful-life impacts classified by expense type. Cash equivalents have purchase maturities of three months or less, unless held in larger investment pools, and hedge-related cash flows are classified according to hedge or instrument purpose and accounting nature.

nodes.title: P. Investments and Derivative Financial Instruments
nodes.summary: The text explains accounting policies for investments and derivatives: classification and measurement of public and private equity, available-for-sale and held-to-maturity debt, equity-method investments, realized gains, impairment, and derivative fair-value changes. Expected insurance recoveries are recorded when assured.

nodes.summary: Share-based compensation grants are generally measured at fair value and expensed over vesting periods. Pfizer acquired Seagen on December 14, 2023, for $44.2 billion ($43.4 billion net of cash); $476 million of employee-award compensation was recorded as acquisition-related expense. The note describes Seagen’s oncology business and strategic benefits, provisional purchase-price allocation and items pending final valuation, tax, inventory, and other information, plus receivables and environmental, legal, and tax contingencies. It explains goodwill’s composition, Biopharma allocation, and non-amortization and non-deductibility. Upjohn Separation and Combination with Mylan

The text describes post-sale arrangements for Meridian and the 2020 Upjohn–Mylan combination, their terms, completion of transitional services, immaterial recorded amounts, balances due to Viatris, and related cash-flow classification. The text provides Haleon’s summarized balance-sheet and income information, and details pre-demerger debt issuance, Pfizer’s indemnity, its loan and repayment, and dividends. nodes.title: D. Licensing Arrangement
nodes.summary: The text presents licensing-arrangement financial figures for 2021–2023, including amounts and deductions, then describes the Valneva agreement. In June 2022, the company invested €90.5 million ($95 million) in Valneva and amended its 2020 VLA15 Lyme disease vaccine co-development and commercialization agreement. Valneva will fund 40% of remaining shared development costs; royalties are tiered at 14%–22%, supplemented by up to $100 million in cumulative-sales milestones, while other early commercialization milestones remain unchanged. At December 31, 2023, the company held a 6.9% Valneva stake.

nodes.title: E. Collaborative Arrangements
key_items: Collaboration with Biohaven; Collaborations with BioNTech; Collaboration with Beam

Details agreements with Biohaven for migraine medicines (later settled through Pfizer’s acquisition of Biohaven); BioNTech for shingles and COVID-19 vaccines, including cost/profit sharing, territorial rights, and equity ownership; Beam for genetic-disease base-editing programs, including licensing options and potential milestones; and Arvinas for ARV-471, with shared costs and profits. Blackstone may receive up to $468 million in approval milestones, up to $550 million in sales milestones, and mid-to-high single-digit sales royalties; milestones are capitalized and amortized, while royalties are cost of sales. Pfizer’s 2019 transformation program covered corporate, commercial, manufacturing, and R&D changes, incurred $4.0 billion through 2023 (including $1.5 billion for Biopharma), and is substantially complete. A cost-realignment program launched in late 2023 targets about $3.0 billion through 2024, mainly severance and implementation; 2023 costs were $1.7 billion, including $674 million for Biopharma.

nodes.title: D. Tax Contingencies
D. Tax Contingencies (intro)
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s 2023 tax-contingency disclosures describe uncertain tax positions, related assets, a 2021–2023 reconciliation of unrecognized tax benefits, accrued interest and penalties, audit jurisdictions and years, and possible near-term reductions and estimation uncertainty. The text also reports 2021–2023 tax effects on other comprehensive income and changes in accumulated other comprehensive loss by category. Finally, it presents 2023 and 2022 recurring fair-value measurements and hierarchy classifications for financial assets and liabilities, with notes on restricted employee-benefit-plan investments and insurance policies.

nodes.title: Financial Assets and Liabilities Not Measured at Fair Value on a Recurring Basis
nodes.summary: The notes disclose fair values and hierarchy levels for debt and other assets/liabilities not regularly measured at fair value. They summarize short- and long-term investments and equity-method holdings, debt-security types, fair values, unrealized gains/losses, maturities, and immaterial expected credit losses; equity-security realized and unrealized gains/losses and adjustments are also reported. Short-term borrowings are detailed by type and carrying amount, including Seagen-related commercial paper, interest rate and collateral information, plus available revolving credit facilities and other credit lines, nearly all unused.

The section covers uncertain tax positions, unrecognized tax benefits and their reconciliation, accrued interest and penalties, audit jurisdictions and periods, possible near-term changes, estimation uncertainty, and tax effects on other comprehensive income and accumulated losses. It also reports recurring fair-value measurements and hierarchy classifications, including restricted benefit-plan investments and insurance policies; fair values and hierarchy levels for assets and liabilities not measured recurrently; investment holdings, debt and equity securities, gains and losses, maturities, and credit losses; and short-term borrowings, interest, collateral, and available credit facilities.

nodes.title: D. Long-Term Debt
nodes.summary: The disclosure lists Pfizer’s senior unsecured long-term debt by maturity and weighted-average stated interest rates for 2023 and 2022, along with principal totals, fair-value adjustments, unamortized discounts/premiums and issuance costs, other debt, carrying amounts, and current portions. Debt was $61.538 billion at December 31, 2023, versus $32.884 billion in 2022. Debt is generally redeemable at varying prices; 2024 notes were reclassified as current. In May 2023, subsidiary PIE issued $31 billion of notes maturing 2025–2063 to help finance Seagen’s acquisition; Pfizer guarantees them, they are callable at make-whole prices, and their issuance weighted-average effective rate was 4.93%. PIE has no other assets or operations. Pfizer also notes its August 2021 issuance of $1 billion in 2031 notes at a 1.79% effective rate.

nodes.title: E. Derivative Financial Instruments and Hedging Activities
nodes.summary: Pfizer describes managing foreign-exchange exposure with derivatives and foreign-currency debt, including hedges of currencies, forecast intercompany inventory sales, and net investments in foreign subsidiaries. It explains accounting for fair-value, cash-flow, net-investment, and non-designated hedges, and managing interest-rate risk with swaps, primarily for U.S.-dollar fixed-rate debt. Tables report derivative fair values, notionals, hedge gains and losses recognized or reclassified through earnings and OCI for 2023–2022, related footnotes and expected reclassifications, and cumulative fair-value hedge basis adjustments to short- and long-term debt.

nodes.title: F. Credit Risk
nodes.summary: Pfizer continually monitors credit risk across customers, financial institutions, and investments. It assesses trade-customer creditworthiness, generally requires no collateral, and notes receivables are concentrated among wholesalers and governments. Investments are primarily short-term, investment-grade, subject to counterparty limits, and mainly exposed to U.S. government funds and debt. Derivatives use ISDA agreements with daily collateral exchange, limiting counterparty concentration; at year-end 2023, net payables of $768 million had $771 million collateral posted, while net receivables of $225 million had $221 million collateral received.

Pfizer’s disclosures cover acquisitions and related pro forma accounting; divestitures, post-sale arrangements and discontinued operations; equity-method investments, licensing, collaborations and R&D funding; and transformation and restructuring programs. They also detail acquisition and productivity costs, other income and impairments, income taxes and tax contingencies, recurring and nonrecurring fair values, investments, borrowings and long-term debt, derivatives and hedging, and credit-risk management.

summary: Pfizer’s notes cover investment accounting, taxes and uncertain tax positions, pensions and postretirement benefits, and legal and environmental contingencies. They describe share-based compensation and acquisitions—including Seagen, GBT, Biohaven, Arena, and ReViral—with transaction accounting, goodwill, assets, liabilities, costs, and pro forma results. Other disclosures address divestitures and discontinued operations; equity-method investments, licensing, collaborations, and R&D funding; restructuring and productivity programs; income, impairments, and fair-value measurements; investments, debt, derivatives, hedging, and credit-risk management.

title: Note 8. Other Financial Information
key_items: A. Inventories; B. Other Current Liabilities; C. Supplier Finance Program Obligation
summary: Note 8 covers inventories, other current liabilities, and supplier finance obligations. Inventory components totaled $10.2 billion in 2023 versus $9.0 billion in 2022; the increase mainly reflects acquired Seagen inventory and product-related increases, partly offset by Paxlovid and Comirnaty write-offs. Noncurrent inventory declined $1.3 billion, chiefly due to those write-offs, partly offset by Seagen inventory; write-offs followed commercial outlook assessments, with no estimated recoverability issues. Other current liabilities included amounts payable to BioNTech for Comirnaty profit sharing of $2.0 billion in 2023 and $5.2 billion in 2022. Under voluntary supplier-finance arrangements, suppliers may sell receivables to banks; Pfizer is not party to their financing, provides no guarantees, and pays confirmed invoices at original maturity, generally within 90–120 days. Outstanding related trade payables were $791 million and $849 million, respectively.

title: Note 9. Property, Plant and Equipment
summary: Note 9 presents Pfizer’s property, plant and equipment by category and useful life: land; buildings (33–50 years); machinery and equipment (8–20 years); furniture, fixtures and other (3–12.5 years); and construction in progress. It gives 2023 and 2022 gross assets, accumulated depreciation, and net property, plant and equipment. It also introduces a geographic breakdown of property, plant and equipment across the United States, Developed Europe, Developed Rest of World, and Emerging Markets, but provides no amounts in the excerpt.

title: Note 10. Identifiable Intangible Assets and Goodwill
summary: The note reports Pfizer’s 2023 and 2022 identifiable intangible assets by finite- and indefinite-lived category, gross carrying value, accumulated amortization and net value. Changes reflect Seagen and other acquisitions, IPR&D transfers and milestones, amortization, and impairments. It explains the nature and accounting treatment of developed technology rights, brands, IPR&D, and licensing agreements, including when amortization begins and impairment risks. Finite-lived assets have an approximately 11-year weighted-average life; expected amortization is provided for 2024–2028. Goodwill balances and changes are reported, including acquisition additions and foreign-exchange effects; goodwill is assigned to Biopharma.

title: Note 11. Pension and Postretirement Benefit Plans and Defined Contribution Plans
key_items: A. Components of Net Periodic Benefit Costs and Changes in Other Comprehensive Income/(Loss)
summary: The note describes Pfizer’s U.S. and global defined benefit, defined contribution, and retiree medical plans, including qualified and supplemental plan distinctions. It reports 2021–2023 pension and postretirement periodic costs or credits and related other comprehensive income, explaining actuarial gains and losses and where non-service costs are recorded. It presents actuarial assumptions by plan and year, explains annual review and discount-rate methods and 2023 changes, and gives U.S. healthcare cost-trend assumptions and projected ultimate-rate years.

title: Pfizer Inc.
key_items: E. Cash Flows; F. Defined Contribution Plans
summary: The notes detail Pfizer’s pension and postretirement benefits: actuarial assumptions and how discount rates and healthcare cost trends are set; changes in benefit obligations, plan assets, funded status and amounts recognized in the balance sheet and accumulated other comprehensive loss; and plan-asset allocations, fair-value levels, valuation methods and investment strategy. They also provide expected contributions and benefit payments, explain funding practices, and describe defined-contribution plans and employer charges. Disclosures include frozen U.S. pension plans, actuarial changes, an annuity buyout, and overfunded plans.

title: Note 12. Equity
summary: Pfizer repurchases common stock through private or open-market transactions under a board-authorized plan. A $10 billion program was authorized in December 2018, with repurchases beginning in 2019; in first-quarter 2022, Pfizer bought 39 million shares for $2 billion, and $3.3 billion remained authorized at year-end 2023. Its Common ESOP shares were fully allocated to U.S. defined-contribution plan participants by December 31, 2023; compensation costs were $20 million in 2023 and $19 million in each of 2022 and 2021.

title: Note 13. Share-Based Payments
summary: Pfizer describes its share-based compensation programs, the 2019 Stock Plan’s authorization, individual grant limits, share-counting rules, available shares, and use of issued or treasury stock. It outlines recipients, terms, vesting, performance conditions, settlement, valuation, and expense recognition for TSRUs, RSUs, PPSs, PSAs, BPAs, and stock options, noting no BPAs granted or outstanding in 2023. Tables report award activity, vesting values, exercises, compensation costs, tax benefits, unrecognized costs and recognition periods, annual expenses, valuation assumptions, and 2023 outstanding awards.

title: TSRUs
summary: The notes describe Pfizer’s stock-option terms, grant-date Black-Scholes valuation, vesting and expense recognition, and report 2021–2023 share-based award activity, compensation costs and tax benefits, unrecognized costs, valuation assumptions, and 2023 TSRU, RSU, PPS, PSA and stock-option activity and outstanding balances. They also summarize TSRU settlements and conversions and provide 2021–2023 EPS calculations, including income, basic and diluted share counts, and anti-dilutive equivalents.

title: Note 15. Leases
summary: Pfizer leases real estate, fleet and equipment, typically for 1–30 years, with some extension or termination options; reasonably certain options are included in lease terms. Some fleet leases have residual-value guarantees, and leases may include variable payments and taxes or other non-lease costs. Variable lease payments were $444 million in 2023, $536 million in 2022 and $381 million in 2021. Pfizer combines lease and non-lease components for all asset classes. It describes lease identification, classification, right-of-use (ROU) assets and liabilities, and use of incremental borrowing rates to measure present value. The note reports balance-sheet lease amounts, lease-cost components, weighted-average terms and discount rates, cash paid and sale-leaseback gains or losses for 2021–2023, and a 2023 maturity reconciliation: $3.824 billion undiscounted payments, $671 million imputed interest, $3.153 billion present value, including $527 million current and $2.626 billion noncurrent liabilities.

title: Note 16. Contingencies and Certain Commitments
key_items: B. Guarantees and Indemnifications; C. Certain Commitments; D. Contingent Consideration for Acquisitions; E. Insurance
summary: Pfizer describes ordinary-course legal, tax, guarantee and indemnity contingencies, noting litigation’s uncertainty, accrual practices, inability to estimate excess losses, and its view that pending matters will not materially affect financial position, though results or cash flows could be affected. It details patent disputes (including Xeljanz, Ibrance, Mektovi, Vyndaqel/Vyndamax, Comirnaty, Paxlovid and Abrysvo), product litigation (asbestos, Effexor, Lipitor, EpiPen, Docetaxel, Zantac and Chantix), commercial/environmental matters, and government investigations. It also summarizes transaction indemnities and guarantees, $5.2 billion in commitments, acquisition contingent consideration of $692 million, and insurance/self-insurance risks.

title: Note 17. Segment, Geographic and Other Revenue Information

nodes.title: A. Segment Information
nodes.summary: Pfizer describes its 2023 operating segments: Biopharma, the sole reportable segment, and newly formed Business Innovation (PC1 and Pfizer Ignite), plus regional selling organizations and shared global functions. It explains the July 2023 shift from WRDM/GPD to oncology-focused ORD and non-oncology PRD R&D organizations, services provided to Biopharma, and costs classified as other business activities or unallocated/reconciling items. Assets are managed company-wide, not by segment; total assets were $227 billion in 2023 versus $197 billion in 2022. Tables report 2021–2023 segment and other-activity revenues, earnings, and depreciation/amortization, with notes on shared-facility depreciation, ViiV dividends, a $3.5 billion 2023 revenue reversal, COVID-19 inventory-related charges, and significant impairments, restructuring, investment gains/losses, and pension gains.

nodes.title: B. Geographic Information
nodes.summary: Geographic revenues (in millions) for 2023, 2022, and 2021 were reported for the United States, developed Europe, developed rest of world, and emerging markets, totaling $58.496 billion, $81.288 billion, and $100.330 billion, respectively. Revenues exceeded $500 million in 14, 24, and 21 countries outside the U.S. in those years. The U.S. was the only country contributing over 10% of total revenue; Japan was the largest outside the U.S., accounting for 6%, 8%, and 9%, respectively.

nodes.title: C. Other Revenue Information

It reports customer revenue concentrations and receivables, lists major product revenues and indications across Biopharma and Business Innovation with explanatory notes, and summarizes remaining performance obligations and deferred revenues for Comirnaty and Paxlovid. It also states there were no accountant disagreements, disclosure controls were effective, and Seagen’s acquisition was the only notable internal-control change.

summary: Describes Pfizer’s operating segments, 2023 organizational and R&D changes, shared functions, company-wide asset management, and 2021–2023 segment revenue, earnings, depreciation and significant adjustments. Reports geographic revenue by region, countries exceeding revenue thresholds, and Japan’s share. Covers major Comirnaty and Paxlovid supply arrangements, customer revenue and receivable concentrations, key product revenues and indications, and remaining performance obligations and deferred revenue. Also addresses accountant disagreements, disclosure-control effectiveness, and internal-control changes following Seagen’s acquisition.

title: Deferred Revenue, Accountants, and Controls
key_items: ITEM 9. CHANGES IN AND DISAGREEMENTS WITH ACCOUNTANTS ON ACCOUNTING AND FINANCIAL DISCLOSURE
summary: Pfizer reports Comirnaty deferred revenue of $1.7 billion at year-end 2023, down from $2.5 billion in 2022, mainly as products were delivered; $2.2 billion of the prior-year balance was recognized in 2023. Paxlovid and Comirnaty deferred revenue will be recognized as performance obligations are met, with current amounts expected within 12 months and noncurrent amounts from December 2024 through 2028; other-product balances were insignificant. There were no accounting or financial disclosure disagreements with accountants. Management found disclosure controls effective. The Seagen acquisition was the only noted change to internal financial reporting controls, with no material impact otherwise.

The report explains management’s and auditors’ responsibilities, audit procedures and reasonable-assurance basis, the purpose and components of financial-reporting controls, and their inherent limitations, including risks of undetected misstatements and future control deterioration. Dated February 22, 2024, in New York.

It describes internal control over financial reporting, its objectives and inherent limitations, and reports that controls were effective as of December 31, 2023, based on the COSO 2013 framework. The assessment excluded Seagen, acquired December 14, 2023; Seagen contributed 0.2% of annual revenue and 22% of year-end assets. Independent auditors issued a report on internal controls. key_items: DESCRIPTION OF THE REGISTRANT’S SECURITIES REGISTERED PURSUANT TO SECTION 12 OF THE SECURITIES EXCHANGE ACT OF 1934
summary: Exhibit 4.26 describes Pfizer Inc.’s securities registered under Exchange Act Section 12 as of February 22, 2024: its common stock and 1.000% Notes due 2027. The descriptions are summaries qualified by Pfizer’s restated certificate of incorporation, bylaws, applicable Delaware law, base indenture, and ninth supplemental indenture, which are referenced for further information. “Pfizer,” “we,” “us,” and “our” refer to Pfizer Inc. unless context indicates otherwise.

title: DESCRIPTION OF CAPITAL STOCK
summary: Pfizer may issue up to 12 billion common shares ($0.05 par) and 27 million no-par preferred shares. Common stock has one vote per share, no redemption, conversion, call, or preemptive rights; dividends are board-declared, liquidation distributions are proportional, outstanding shares are fully paid and nonassessable, and the stock trades as PFE on the NYSE. The board sets preferred-stock series terms and quantities. Charter and bylaws may impede control changes through restrictions on special meetings and written consent, board authority over preferred stock, rights plans, board size, and vacancies. Delaware’s Section 203 generally restricts business combinations with 15%-or-more interested stockholders for three years unless specified board, ownership, and shareholder-approval conditions are met, potentially delaying or discouraging takeovers.

title: DESCRIPTION OF DEBT SECURITIES

nodes.title: DESCRIPTION OF DEBT SECURITIES (intro)

Covers denominations, interest calculation and record dates, payment agents and book-entry channels; euro payments and dollar substitution if euros become unavailable; additional-payment tax protection and its exceptions and U.S. tax definitions; unsecured, unsubordinated ranking and NYSE listing; limited merger/conveyance covenant, absence of other protections, and conditions for issuing fungible additional notes. Describes optional redemption prices, notice, selection and settlement mechanics, benchmark definitions, no sinking fund, and whole-series tax redemption rights.

nodes.title: Global Clearance and Settlement
nodes.summary: The notes are issued as registered global notes held by a common depositary for Euroclear and Clearstream; certificates are generally unavailable, and global notes may be transferred only in whole to those systems or their nominees. Beneficial interests are held through participant accounts in specified denominations, and system records determine holders, subject to payment rights of the registered holder. The text disclaims responsibility for system information, then describes Clearstream’s Luxembourg regulation, services, participants, Euroclear link and distribution procedures, and Euroclear’s history, operator, rules under Belgian law, fungible holdings, participant access and distribution procedures.

nodes.title: Euroclear and Clearstream Arrangements
nodes.summary: While Euroclear, Clearstream, or their nominee or common depositary is registered holder of the global notes, it is treated as their sole holder, receives payments, and distributions are credited in euros to customer cash accounts under system rules. Pfizer, the trustee, and related parties are not responsible for beneficial-ownership records or payments. Because investors hold interests through clearing-system participants and indirect participants, the absence of physical certificates may limit their ability to pledge interests or take other actions.

nodes.title: Secondary Market Trading
nodes.summary: Secondary-market note trades between Clearstream and Euroclear participants follow each system’s rules and conventional eurobond settlement procedures. Parties should confirm their account locations when trading because the purchaser determines delivery location and this affects settlement timing. Deliveries, payments, and communications are possible only when the relevant system is open; differing holidays and time zones may delay U.S.-initiated transactions until the next business day in Luxembourg or Brussels. The systems credit payments and take other permitted holder actions under their rules, and may discontinue these facilitation procedures at any time.

nodes.title: Exchange of Global Notes for Certificated Notes

It describes indenture amendments requiring majority consent and changes requiring each affected holder’s consent; Events of Default, acceleration and rescission, waiver rules, trustee duties and holder directions, and the annual officers’ certificate. It also outlines optional full or covenant defeasance through an irrevocable deposit of sufficient cash or government securities, subject to certification and legal-opinion conditions.

It also permits eligible Pfizer and Wyeth sub-plan participants to make a one-time in-service transfer of their full non-grandfathered benefit lump sum to the PSSP. Eligibility differs by sub-plan; amounts use August 1, 2023 actuarial assumptions, with no interim interest adjustment, and retain the original payment timing and form. title: Certification by the Chief Executive Officer Pursuant to Section 302 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002
summary: Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla’s February 22, 2024, Sarbanes-Oxley Section 302 certification states that he reviewed the company’s Form 10-K; believes it contains no material misstatements or omissions and fairly presents its financial condition, results, and cash flows; and, with the other certifying officer, is responsible for disclosure controls and financial reporting controls. They designed and evaluated those controls, reported material control changes, and disclosed significant deficiencies, material weaknesses, and relevant fraud to the auditors and audit committee.

nodes.title: EXHIBIT 32.1
nodes.summary: Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla certifies under Section 906 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act that the company’s 2023 Form 10-K complies with applicable Exchange Act requirements and fairly presents, in all material respects, Pfizer’s financial condition and operating results. Signed February 22, 2024, the certification accompanies the report but is not deemed filed under Exchange Act Section 18 or incorporated by reference into other filings unless legally required or specifically incorporated.

nodes.title: EXHIBIT 32.2
nodes.summary: Exhibit 32.2 is Pfizer CFO David M. Denton’s certification under 18 U.S.C. § 1350 and Sarbanes-Oxley Act Section 906. He certifies that Pfizer’s 2023 Form 10-K complies with applicable Securities Exchange Act reporting requirements and fairly presents, in all material respects, the company’s financial condition and operating results. Signed February 22, 2024, the certification accompanies the report but is not deemed filed under Exchange Act Section 18 or incorporated by reference into other filings unless legally required or specifically incorporated.

nodes.title: EXHIBIT 97
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s policy, adopted under Dodd-Frank and SEC/NYSE rules, defines covered compensation, executives, financial measures, restatements, and a three-year lookback. Following a qualifying restatement, excess incentive compensation must be forfeited if unpaid or promptly repaid, except in specified impracticability cases; recovery methods include notice, offsets, and award forfeiture. The policy bars indemnification, assigns administration and amendment authority to the Committee or Board, addresses compliance, enforceability and interaction with other recovery rights, and binds successors and beneficiaries.

summary: The section includes Pfizer’s CFO’s Section 302 certification that he reviewed the 2023 Form 10-K, believes it is materially accurate and fairly presents the company’s financial position and results, and shares responsibility for disclosure and financial-reporting controls, including reporting deficiencies and relevant fraud. CEO and CFO Section 906 certifications affirm the report’s regulatory compliance and fair presentation; they accompany but generally are not deemed filed or incorporated into other filings. Exhibit 97 sets out the company’s executive compensation recovery policy, including covered compensation, restatement triggers, recovery procedures and exceptions, administration, enforceability, and limits on indemnification.

title: ACKNOWLEDGMENT, CONSENT AND AGREEMENT
summary: The acknowledgment confirms receipt and review of Pfizer’s Recoupment Policy, an opportunity to ask questions and consult counsel, and voluntary, irrevocable agreement to comply, including repaying required Erroneously Awarded Compensation. It acknowledges that compensation from the Company Group is subject to the Policy and may be affected, and that no indemnification, insurance, or reimbursement is available for compensation subject to recoupment or forfeiture. Undefined capitalized terms follow the Policy. Signature, printed-name, and date fields are provided.
